implementation_notes: TypeScript's load-levelling default is the same in-process promise queue as JavaScript, with types: a PQueue<Job> (p-queue is itself written in TypeScript) runs at most {concurrency} task functions at once and buffers the rest, exposing size and pending for backlog metrics. The queue is the buffer, the concurrency option is the drain rate, and the generic typing of the task closures keeps the job contract checked at compile time. It is bounded only by memory and lost on restart, so it fits request-path smoothing; durable work belongs on the Redis-backed variant.
pitfalls: The concurrency limit is per process: running several instances multiplies the real rate at the dependency.
Type parameters do not survive serialization - if the queue ever moves out of process the compile-time contract is gone and runtime validation is required.
An unhandled rejection from add() can terminate the process; attach handling at the call site.
In-memory queue means a deploy drops the backlog; durable work needs BullMQ or equivalent.

variants.name: BullMQ typed Queue/Worker pair over Redis
variants.implementation_notes: For durable, horizontally scaled queueing, BullMQ with TypeScript generics gives one contract for both ends: Queue<DataType, ResultType> adds jobs and Worker<DataType> consumes them with its own concurrency setting, while Redis holds the backlog. Retries, exponential backoff, priorities, delayed jobs and the failed set replace the hand-rolled retry/DLQ layer, and worker processes can be added independently of producers (at-least-once in the worst case, per the project's own goal statement). Choose it when accepted work must survive restarts or when several services share one queue; keep p-queue for in-process smoothing.
variants.idiom_name: BullMQ Queue<T>/Worker<T> with typed job data
pitfalls: Generic types are compile-time only: a producer deployed with a changed JobData shape breaks consumers of already-queued jobs unless a version field is carried in the payload.
Worker concurrency multiplied by replica count is the real downstream load - the queue does not cap it by itself.
At-least-once delivery requires idempotent processors, keyed by job id or a business idempotency key.
Redis configuration (persistence, eviction, memory limits) decides whether accepted work survives a restart.
